Suppose that we have an IRF $\{\phi_t\}_{t=1}^T$.

The idea is to classify the sign of an IRF by the area under the curve described by its trajectory.

In that sense, we need to measure the area above and below the horizontal axis, as well as the total net area.
$$
\begin{align}
A^{+} &= \sum_{t=1}^T \max(\phi_t, 0)\\
A^{-} &= \sum_{t=1}^T \max(-\phi_t, 0)\\
A &= A^{+} + A^{-}
\end{align}
$$

Then we need to establish a criterion to classify an IRF. This is the purpose of the function $s$:

$$
s(A^{+}, A^{-}, A; \delta, \eta) = \begin{cases}
1, & A < \delta\\
2, & A \geq \delta \land \dfrac{A^{+}}{A} \geq 1 - \eta\\
3, & A \geq \delta \land \dfrac{A^{-}}{A} \geq 1 - \eta\\
4, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

The parameter $\delta$ defines a tolerance level used to classify a non-response. This is useful because the representation of zero is often approximate. On the other hand, the parameter $\eta \in [0, 1]$ represents the amount of area of the opposite sign allowed to be present in the IRF.

The categories are mapped as follows:

- $s(.) = 1$: No response.
- $s(.) = 2$: Mainly positive response.
- $s(.) = 3$: Mainly negative response.
- $s(.) = 4$: Mixed response.

Each category follows from the common intuition used to classify IRFs according to the sign of the response.
